svg.title: Three kinds of leak, and why collapsing them is the mistake
svg.desc: A leak you chose, a leak the stack chose for you, and a leak nobody chose and everyone inherited. Each has a different fix, a different owner, and a different obligation on whoever describes it.
svg.text: Three kinds of leak
Most privacy writing collapses these into one. They have different fixes, different owners, and different obligations.
A leak
you chose
You are the one who
can change it.
In this build: you answer an address request with a public account id rather than a shielded receiving key.
Anyone reading the chain sees the payment. The choice is deliberately the payee's, and it comes first.
What would change it: nothing but a different choice. A payer cannot upgrade a public destination to a private
one — the address form is what a rail can reach, not a preference.
The obligation: say what it costs at the moment of choosing, not in a panel someone has to go and open.
A leak the stack
chose for you
Not yours to fix, and
not the app's either.
In this build: one content topic per conversation. A store node sees which topics this client subscribes to
and when it publishes or fetches — the contact graph, pseudonymously. End-to-end encryption does not touch it.
What would change it: a mixnet at the transport layer. Not an application change, and not Tor — Tor hides
who by IP, not what links to what. Running your own store node is not a fix either: it protects the operator's own
metadata, not their peers', and it lets an operator learn when a target fetches.
The obligation: name the fix and its real status. LOGOS-MIXNET is a LIP at status `raw`, implemented
send-only, and absent from the near-term roadmap. "Coming soon" is not a status.
A leak nobody
chose
Inherited. Everyone
on the network has it.
In this build: the anonymity set is small because the network is young — a demo with two users is the
smallest one there is. Every shielded transfer is unlinkable to every other, and there are only two people it could
have been between. No amount of cryptography closes that; only other users do.
What would change it: time and adoption. Nothing in this repository, and nothing upstream either —
which is what makes it the honest example of the class rather than a bug wearing the class as a costume.
The obligation: do not present an inherited limit as a design — nor a misdiagnosis as an inherited limit.
Three different fixes, three different owners, three different things a reader can do about it.
A write-up that calls all three "privacy trade-offs" has told you nothing about which one you can act on.
